sections.heading: What is the Monotonic Queue Pattern?
sections.content: A monotonic queue is a double-ended queue (deque) whose elements stay sorted in one direction, either decreasing or increasing from front to back. It is used with a sliding window. New elements are added at the back after removing every element that can never become the answer again. Old elements leave from the front when they slide out of the window. The front of the deque always holds the current window's maximum (or minimum) in O(1). Each element enters and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n).

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Find the maximum or minimum of every sliding window of size K
Find the longest subarray where max - min is within a limit
Optimize a DP where each state depends on the best value in a moving window
Find the shortest subarray with sum at least K when negatives exist
Any problem needing a running max or min over a range that moves forward
Keywords: sliding window maximum, window minimum, at most limit, within K steps, jump game with window

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Imagine the window as a line of people and you want the tallest person at any time. If a taller person arrives behind a shorter one, the shorter person can never be the tallest again, because the taller one will stay in the window at least as long. So you remove the shorter people from the back. The person at the front is always the tallest, and when they walk out of the window you remove them from the front.

Why Store Indices, Not Values
items: You must know when the front element leaves the window (index <= i - k)
You can still read the value with nums[index]
For a variable window, compare the front index with the left pointer
Storing values only works if duplicates and expiry do not matter (rare)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Storing values instead of indices, so you cannot tell when an element expires
Forgetting to remove expired front indices before reading the max
Reading the front before the first window is full (i < k - 1)
Using a stack-like pattern when the window must remove old elements from the front
Using < and <= inconsistently, which can drop equal values that are still needed
Calling first() or last() on an empty deque
Not using Long for prefix sums when values are large
Using a sorted structure (TreeMap or PriorityQueue) when a deque gives O(n) instead of O(n log n)

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: A monotonic queue is a deque that keeps its values sorted, giving the window max or min at the front
Each step: expire old indices from the front, clean the back, add the new index, read the front
Decreasing deque gives the maximum, increasing deque gives the minimum
Always store indices so you can detect expired elements
Use two deques when you need both the max and the min of a window
Each index enters and leaves once, so the time is O(n)
